en: Went along the road.
Who dwelt in Eki-Kemin,
Called an untroubled hero,
Who had been alone and gained a following,
Who had been poor and grown rich,
Who kept twin black horses tethered,
Who sharpened his black tongue,
Who made a dark cave his house,
Who made the dense forest his wealth,
Hero Ürbü of the Kyrgyz,
He too went along the road,
With a numerous host.
Who dwelt in Kebez-Too,
Called a stately hero,
Who kept Chalkuyruk tethered,
Who readied his host for battle,
The hero among heroes, Er Töshtük,
The youngest of nine sons,
A servant of the one God,
He too went with his host.
Who dwelt in Chong-Alay,
Called a fearless hero,
Who trained a harrier into a hunting hawk,
Who gathered disparate people into a nation,
Who reared a little falcon into a hunting hawk,
Who made a people of wanderers,
Khan Shygay, who dwelt in Altay,
He too went along the road,
With a host numbering a vast multitude.
The Sarts, the people of four khans, came.
No people to bind and support the waist,
They came as an affliction of back pain;
Dust rising to the sky came.
Mounting from distant lands,
They came from India too.
On a road opened by saints,
As twelve vast hosts,
With right and left wings complete,
They set off toward Beijing.
People of many tribes came;
Khans who led peoples came.
“The red banner with its golden crescent
I shall carry before them,” he said.
“If any die upon the campaign,
I shall stand for their funeral rites,” he said.
Aykojo of Andijan,
He too now went along.
Having his gray wondrous steed led beside him,
Loading baggage on several horses,
Taking a coat no bullet could pierce,
His nobility worth many multitudes,
Khan Bakay, surpassing in sound judgment,
“Do not turn back and leave,” he said,
“Do not incur the khan's wrath,” he said,
“Drive them all, leaving none,” he said.
Bakay traveled at the rear.
At that time, Khan Manas,
Akolpok, which no bullet could pierce,
And coats of that kind,
Had twelve of them folded
And loaded upon Zhelmayan.
The black camel with its broad hump,
No wind could match its trot;
No animal could match its walk.
When going on a distant journey,
When wreaking havoc on the enemy,
Zhelmayan carried ammunition.
From the dark eye of the spring,
From the very plane tree,
From Khan Manas's court,
From the royal fortress,
From the garden before it,
From sovereign Manas's throne,
He rode forth in stately grandeur.
All his arms and armor,
Khan Manas, from Kanykey,
Stood tall and requested.
May whoever calls her merely a woman not prosper!
Those who call her merely a woman,
May their number never become two!
All the equipment,
Had she not put it in order?
The clothing to wear in a firefight,
Had she not made it ready?
At Khan Manas's Akolpok,
As Kanykey bit the thread,
Her front teeth were worn away.
As she gazed intently at Akolpok,
Her black eyes were hollowed out.
To Kokand and Tashkent,
While her reach extended,
Over Alty-Shaar and Samarkand,
While her power extended,
She sent searching through Andijan,
Had white cotton and silk brought,
And filings of hard iron
Gathered and brought from the smiths,
Had them placed between its layers.
Making it thoroughly, she left it long:
“When sixty Chinese, a thousand governors,
Come forth to exchange fire,
Let no bullet pass through,” she said.
Dividing and twisting it twelvefold,
Akolpok, Kanykey
Made ready over twelve years.
When Manas wore it, it was roomy;
All twelve parts fitted evenly.
The head of the forty, old Kyrgyl,
The red old man, puffed up at forty,
The clear-minded old man of a good father,
Except for his ignorance,
An old man senior to the forty warriors,
Morning and evening, evil
Was the thought of that wicked old man.
“Along the waters of Keng-Kol,” he said,
“Kanykey and Chubak
Are passionate lovers,” he said.
When he twisted truthful speech,
When he harbored wickedness,
When Khan Manas would no longer lie with her,
And neglected her for six months,
Without rest by day,
Without sleep at night,
She made it with all her heart.
From the torment of gossip,
Her tears became a lake.
When she had sewn Akolpok,
She became Manas's equal again.
Akolpok that Kanykey sewed:
Golden collar, copper sleeves,
Double-layered mail with lark-eye rings,
A netted outer garment, a broad coat.
Walking silently, grieving,
Her moon-like face shining,
The great earrings made of gold
Clattered against her breast.
Bracing it with rods in seven separate parts,
Had she not twisted it?
To Beijing, seven months away,
When he reached it and joined battle,
“A bullet might strike him,” she thought,
“Death might suddenly reach him,” she thought.
Akolpok, carefully fashioned,
Its golden collar gleaming—
If you looked at every aspect,
It suited your sultan, Khan Manas.
“I give it as a gift; take it along.
You have set out campaigning against Beijing;
The gilded Bozkise,
Fasten it around your waist as you go!”
Last autumn,
On the plain beyond Alay,
Sixty Russians, measuring the land,
At the time they came out—
Akkelte, seized from them,
Ochogor when at play,
Akkelte when in earnest,
The comfort of a life held in trust,
Akkelte when slung upon the shoulder,
The mirror of the moon-like shoulder-blade—
Kanykey brought and gave it.
At that time, Khan Manas,
Girding on a silver belt,
Light touching his sun-like face,
His front teeth like a great door
Shining in his mouth,
His eyes showing their fierce glint,
Venom pouring from his face—
If one looked closely at Manas,
He seemed like the taker of souls.
Clouds gathered in the sky;
Sixty cares came upon his head at once.
“If I go to Beijing and die,
What will her nights be like?” he thought.
“If this Kanykey is left a widow,
My child left behind is young—
What will his days be like?” he thought.
“Piebald-headed horses upon the hills,
My son behind me is young.
If I should suddenly die,
The six wicked ones will stand in command.
When my eyes have closed,
Will they plunder the goods?
Will they stir up trouble?
Will those pigs destroy my line?
Will they break into my treasury?
When I look at the queen,
Her forehead bone curves back somewhat.
After my eyes have closed,
Her means of living will be scant.”
After hearing Manas's words,
She stood crying shrilly,
Her tears becoming a flood,
Sobbing and wailing like a camel calf.
On hearing the khan's words,
From her dear eyes like blackcurrants,
Tears mingled with blood flowed.
From her eyes like a camel calf's,
Tears flowed in separate streams.
“If you go to Beijing, you will die.
When will you see this poor soul again?
From Beijing, six months away,
When will you return?
My precious noble sovereign,
When will you see your child again?
Beijing, six months away,
You called a journey of six days.
You said you were mighty in the world;
You said, ‘See the people of Beijing.’
Do not let them strike from a flanking way.
By putting them to hardship, my sovereign,
All the champions,
Do not let the Chinese take them as a gift.
Scout the road to Beijing as you go;
Keep me in your heart as you go.
Great Beijing, toward which you head,
They call a journey of five months;
They say its people outnumber mankind.
Those who go do not turn back;
No living person returns.
They call it a land of no return;
They say the Chinese people swarm in hives.
Farewell, be safe, leopard!
The Muslims, not even a world's worth,
You are leaving without that number.
To Beijing, mighty in calamity,
You are leaving despite all pleas.
Scout the road to Beijing and return, my lord;
Burulcha, Esenkan's daughter,
Ask for her as a gift and bring her, my lord!”
Your wolf-maned sovereign Manas,
After hearing Kanykey's words,
Strength sprang from his toil-worn body;
The hair on his face bristled upright.
His eyes blazed like a lion's;
His thirst for blood seized him.
He resolved to go to Beijing,
To the great multitude of Chinese.
Seeing this, the forty warriors,
In tamarisk-grown Keng-Kol, broad Talas,
Had they not been camped?
With marten-fur caps set proudly high,
The warriors swaying about,
In merry, jubilant revelry,
The warriors enjoying themselves—
All forty made ready together.
Into Khan Manas's presence,
They entered in a crowd.
“God knows whether in Talas
You will come and alight again,
Whether after this, from my hands,
You will return and eat again.”
Relating her spoken words,
She brought them into the court,
With Khan Manas at their head.
Entertaining the forty warriors,
